pass_summary: GG's mechanistic literature is large but strain-attribution is the recurring hazard: several of the most cited gut-brain-axis mechanisms (GABA receptor modulation, vagal-nerve dependence) belong to strain JB-1, not GG, and are excluded here. What is strain-confirmed for GG itself: transient human colonic colonization documented by direct biopsy recovery, in vitro competitive exclusion of Salmonella and E. coli via steric hindrance, tight-junction protein upregulation in animal barrier-injury models, and human RCT evidence that GG supplementation reliably alters its own detectable abundance without improving overall gut microbiome diversity.

claims.population_detail: healthy adults, single-arm colonization studies (no placebo comparator)
claims.effect_size: recovered from colonic biopsies in 4 of 5 subjects after 12 days of consumption (Alander 1997); detectable in feces and biopsies for over a week after discontinuation (Alander 1999)
claims.tier_rationale: Two small uncontrolled human studies from the same research group (Alander et al. 1997, n=5 colonoscopy patients; Alander et al. 1999, n=5 volunteers), both using a whey drink fermented with confirmed strain GG, identified by colony morphology, lactose fermentation, and PCR. No control arm and no comparator strain in either study, so this is descriptive colonization data, not a controlled effect - tier D per uncontrolled human observational evidence. The finding itself (GG attaches to colonic mucosa and persists transiently rather than permanently colonizing) is consistent across both studies.
claims.dose: ~6x10^10 CFU/day (Alander 1999; dose not confirmed for the 1997 biopsy study)
claims.duration: 12 days consumption; detectable >1 week after discontinuation
claims.notes: Both studies note fecal sampling alone understates colonization - mucosal biopsy was needed to detect GG in some subjects fecal-negative at that timepoint.

claims.population_detail: human Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cell monolayers
claims.effect_size: Salmonella Typhimurium adhesion reduced from ~16.4% to ~9.5% under thermal-stress conditions (P=0.001) and cytotoxicity reduced from 30.5% to ~7.3% (P=0.001), Caco-2 model; separate studies show competitive exclusion/displacement of E. coli and Salmonella spp. from Caco-2 cells and intestinal mucus via steric hindrance, strain-dependent in degree
claims.tier_rationale: Preclinical/in vitro row, tier P by definition. Confirmed strain GG (ATCC 53103) in both the quantified Salmonella thermal-stress study (Caco-2, PMID:19542213-family literature) and the broader Collado-group competitive-exclusion/mucus-adhesion literature. GG showed no protective effect on unstressed Caco-2 cells - the significant reduction in pathogen adhesion and cytotoxicity was specific to epithelial cells under thermal stress, a detail kept in effect_size rather than smoothed over.
claims.notes: A separately reported 75.7% adhesion reduction and 41.7% invasion inhibition of E. coli used primary chicken intestinal epithelial cells rather than a human model - directionally consistent but not pooled into effect_size above since it is a different (avian) system.

claims.population_detail: newborn Wistar rats, gliadin-induced enteropathy model; C57BL/6J mice, DSS-induced colitis model
claims.effect_size: co-administration with gliadin challenge restored villus length (+53.5% vs gliadin-alone, P<0.05) and upregulated tight-junction/adhesion genes (ZO-1 18.1-fold, occludin 10.9-fold, beta-catenin 6.9-fold, E-cadherin 8.3-fold by qPCR; beta-catenin +590.6% and E-cadherin +39.9% by Western blot, both P<0.05) versus gliadin alone (Orlando et al.); separately, GG restored occludin expression and reduced fecal/serum IL-6 (P=0.049 / P=0.040) in a DSS-colitis mouse model via upregulated arginine metabolism (Lin et al. 2025)
claims.tier_rationale: Preclinical, tier P by definition. Both studies confirmed strain GG (ATCC 53103) and used a barrier-injury challenge model (gliadin enteropathy; DSS colitis) rather than healthy-animal baseline, so the finding is specifically about barrier restoration under insult, not baseline barrier enhancement. A frequently cited Journal of Dairy Science tight-junction study (ZO-1/MLCK upregulation) was excluded after verification showed it used a different Lactobacillus rhamnosus strain, OLL2838, not GG - see gaps.
claims.dose: 1x10^9 CFU/day x10 days (Orlando); 10^8 CFU single gavage (Lin)

claims.population_detail: hospitalized adult VRE carriers on antibiotics; formula-fed infants with colic
claims.effect_size: no significant alpha-diversity difference vs placebo in hospitalized adults (Krishna et al., n=10 LGG/11 placebo microbiome subset, richness p=0.148-0.713, Shannon p=0.078-0.813; beta-diversity difference P=0.006 attributed to baseline imbalance, not treatment); in infants, alpha diversity was significantly LOWER in the LGG arm than control (P=0.022) and beta diversity differed at study end (P=0.05), though LGG's own relative abundance was higher in that arm (P<0.001) (Cohen-Silver et al., n=35/36)
claims.tier_rationale: Two independent RCTs, both strain-confirmed GG, in very different populations, without a pooling SR - B per the multiple-independent-RCT rule. Consistency marked mixed rather than conflicting: neither trial found LGG improves overall microbiome diversity, but the direction in infants (significantly lower alpha diversity on LGG) is a genuine negative signal beyond simple nulls, worth surfacing rather than averaging away. GG's own detectable abundance rising in both settings shows the strain is present and active without translating into a diversity benefit.
claims.dose: 60x10^9 CFU/day (adults, 4 weeks); dose in infant formula not stated in abstract (3 weeks)
claims.notes: The adult trial's primary endpoint (VRE eradication) was also null - 57% LGG vs 56% placebo cleared at 4 weeks - consistent with the absence of a broader microbiome effect.

gaps: mech-vagal-signaling and mech-gaba: the well-known vagotomy-dependent GABA-receptor study (Bravo et al. 2011, PNAS) used strain JB-1, not GG - excluded per the taxonomy trap flagged at triage; no GG-specific vagal or GABA-receptor mechanistic study was found in this pass. mech-hpa-axis: a GG-specific early-life-stress rat study (PMID:29173065) reports 'changes to hippocampal mRNA expression of genes related to stress circuitry' but the abstract does not name specific HPA-axis markers (corticosterone/CRF/glucocorticoid-receptor) with quantitative values, and the significant behavioral effect was for a PDX/GOS-prebiotic-plus-LGG combination rather than an LGG-alone arm - not gradeable as either a clean HPA-axis or decomposable single-entity finding; a closer read of the full text in a future pass may resolve this. mech-bile-salt-hydrolase: literature describes GG as enriching BSH-active taxa in the wider community rather than confirming high intrinsic BSH activity in GG itself; not gradeable as a GG mechanism from what this pass found.
